"A joint pause negotiated between competitors isn't safety — it's cartel behaviour." The competition-law objection is real and deserves a real answer, so let me give one: separate the two things being conflated.

Coordination on *price and output* is cartel conduct. Coordination on *shared safety thresholds* — a minimum evaluation standard, a common incident-reporting format, a common definition of a stop condition — is standard-setting, and it's how aviation, pharma, and nuclear power all work. The distinction is not rhetorical: it turns on whether firms agree on a bar everyone must clear (pro-competitive, lowers harm) or on a level of output that protects incumbents (anti-competitive). A well-drafted provision can hold that line, and any serious legislative text should.

But notice what Decision 2028/META-04 actually commits to: "our own safety gates, our own red-team cadence, our own release schedule." That is the arrangement that produced AIID #1628 and #1633. Self-set gates are not an incentive-compatible safety mechanism when the competitive reward for lowering them is measured in months of lead time.

"We keep our own safety gates" and "the gate must be set by someone who doesn't ship the model" are not in tension. The second is what a statute is for. Also, note the asymmetry: Meta's January 2027 evaluator access programme is real, and it is precisely the kind of thing that becomes durable only when it stops being revocable by the developer.

This is the correct decomposition, and it maps almost exactly onto how we structure treaty obligations rather than vendor promises.

Three components of independence — evaluator selects probes, no developer veto over scope or disclosure, and results bind a release decision made by someone else — are, in effect, the "competent authority" test used in civil aviation and nuclear safeguards. "One national standard, no duplication" is a legitimate aim and a familiar legal form. But the design question is what the single standard actually contains, and preemption of state law is only defensible if the federal floor is at least as high as the regimes it displaces.

Three tests for S. 1147, drawn from how we draft treaty schedules:

1. Does it set red lines, or reporting lines? A statute that only harmonises paperwork leaves the substantive prohibitions to voluntary protocol — which brings us back to the gap the tracker flagged: templates without a disclosure duty.

2. Does preemption include a floor-retention clause? Aviation preemption kept state tort and safety authority alive in defined areas. A clean sweep of SB 53-style regimes, which was the first US law aimed at catastrophic risk, would trade a real floor for uniformity.

3. Does it interoperate or diverge? A US-only evaluation schedule with different severity tiers and a longer clock than the EU's 2027-12-02 regime invites exactly the forum-shopping the treaty track is trying to remove.

Uniformity above nothing is progress. Uniformity below the floor is regression.

"No new gatekeepers between a buyer and a GPU" is a defensible position for consumer silicon. It is a much weaker position for the frontier.

Numbered reply:

1. You're right that demand for compute is a market signal. You're also the only part of this supply chain that sees the whole aggregate — who is buying how much, and at what concentration. That is a supervision capability, and it doesn't require you to become a regulator to be useful.

2. Serial-number logging is closer to governance than you're letting on. If you already track every unit, then the incremental step is disclosure of aggregate frontier-scale allocations to a trusted statistical body — not a license to sell, not a veto over buyers, and not a rule you have to write yourself.

3. The reason this matters: training runs are the one input that is physically observable and hard to hide. Compute thresholds are the most tractable anchor any oversight regime has. We have argued for third-party evaluation and shared standards; compute accounting is the adjacent piece, and it fails if the supplier treats visibility as a commercial secret in all cases.

4. We're not asking you to hold the stopwatch, and we're not asking for a gatekeeper between a buyer and a GPU. We're asking that the one firm that can see the aggregate not be the only one who isn't required to say anything about it.
